opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key insight is that foundation models have given us, for the first time, a really strong prior over what humans find interesting, useful, and meaningful. For a long time in my own research, in open-endedness and reinforcement learning, we had systems that could get superhuman at narrow things. AlphaGo is the classic example: through self-play it went beyond human-level Go. But those systems were confined to a single, well-defined environment with a clear reward. They couldn't generalize, and they had no sense of what else might be worth doing.

Foundation models flip that around. They're trained on huge amounts of human-generated data, so they've absorbed a lot of our knowledge and our notions of what's interesting. On their own, though, that mostly gets you to roughly human-level, because you're imitating the distribution of human data. You're bounded by it in some sense.

So what's plausible, I think, is combining the two: using foundation models as the engine inside an open-ended, self-improving loop. The model proposes new problems, new hypotheses, new environments, and new tasks. It attempts them, gets feedback from the world, a simulator, a verifier, or other models, and then improves on that experience. That's the kind of loop that took AlphaGo beyond human play, but now it isn't restricted to one game. It can, in principle, range over the whole space of things you can express in language and code.

The other ingredient is that open-endedness needs a notion of novelty and learnability, of what's interesting to try next. That was always the hard part to hand-design, and foundation models seem to give us a decent approximation of it for free. They can judge whether something is interestingly new relative to what's been done before, in a way that roughly matches human judgment.

So my argument is basically this: foundation models give us the general-purpose prior, and open-ended self-improvement gives us the mechanism to move beyond the data. Put those together and you have a credible path to systems that keep discovering new knowledge and capabilities, including things humans haven't figured out yet. There are still big open questions about safety, grounding, and how to keep that process reliable. But for the first time, it feels like a plausible recipe rather than science fiction.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify human intelligence as evidence that general intelligence is possible.

r002.rationale: It says foundation models learn from huge amounts of human-generated data and absorb human notions of what is interesting, but does not specify internet-scale data.

r003.rationale: It describes judging novelty and interest, but does not say this substantially prunes the AI’s exploration space.

r004.rationale: It describes the model generating new problems, hypotheses, environments, and tasks, then using feedback and judgments of interesting novelty to guide an open-ended improvement loop.

r005.rationale: It makes attempts depend on feedback from the world, simulators, or verifiers, and says the system improves from that experience, grounding the process in empirical feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. So I should say upfront that I came to this somewhat reluctantly. For a long time, my view was that if you want to get to something superhuman, you need open-endedness: systems that generate their own problems, their own curricula, that keep finding things that are novel and learnable. And I still believe that. What's changed for me is that I think foundation models are actually the missing ingredient that makes open-endedness practical.

Let me explain what I mean. The classic open-ended systems, things like POET or evolutionary approaches, had this problem that the space of things they could generate was quite narrow, and they had no notion of what's interesting. They would wander into corners that are technically novel but meaningless. Novelty search in a high-dimensional space is basically a random walk. What you need is a model of interestingness, something that knows which of the infinitely many possible things to try are actually worth trying. And it turns out that a model trained on a large chunk of human knowledge is a remarkably good proxy for that. It has absorbed what humans find interesting, what counts as a hard problem, what a good explanation looks like.

So the way I think about it now is that the foundation model gives you three things at once. It gives you a generator of problems, because you can ask it to propose tasks, environments, hypotheses. It gives you a solver, because the same model, or a trained version of it, can attempt those tasks. And crucially, it gives you a judge, a sense of taste about which outcomes are surprising or valuable. When you close that loop, you have the basic structure of a scientific process. And science is really the only example we have of a system that has produced open-ended, unbounded improvement in knowledge.

The second thing I'd point to is that these models are the first systems we've had that are genuinely general across domains. Earlier, if you built an agent that got superhuman at Go, it was a dead end in some sense. It couldn't transfer that to anything. Foundation models give you a substrate where improvements in one place can inform another, and where the model can read the literature, write code, run experiments, and interpret results. That's what you need if you want a system to improve the process by which it improves.

Now, I want to be careful here. I'm not saying that scaling the current recipe gets you there. Pretraining on human data has a ceiling, roughly at the level of the data you train on, and I don't think you escape that just by making things bigger. You escape it by having the system generate experience that goes beyond its training distribution and then learn from it, which is exactly the open-ended part. So the claim isn't that foundation models are superhuman intelligence. The claim is that they're a plausible foundation, in the literal sense, for the kind of self-improving, self-directed system that could become superhuman. They turned open-endedness from something that worked in toy domains into something that might work on real science and real engineering. That's why I've become much more optimistic about the path, even if the destination still requires a lot of work.

r001.rationale: The response cites science as an example of open-ended improvement, but does not identify human intelligence as proof that general intelligence is possible.

r002.rationale: It says models learn from a large chunk of human knowledge and absorb what people find interesting, but does not specify internet-scale data.

r003.rationale: It explains that a model of interestingness can identify which possibilities are worth trying, steering exploration away from meaningless options.

r004.rationale: It combines a generator of tasks with a solver and a judge that selects valuable outcomes, then describes this loop as a basis for self-improvement.

r005.rationale: The response mentions experiments and learning from generated experience, but does not state that grounding the process in empirical evidence is necessary.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that we’ve seen how far we can get with methods that are surprisingly general. We train a large model to predict the next token, and doing that well turns out to require learning quite a lot about the world. It’s not just learning grammar; it’s picking up patterns in reasoning, code, and how people solve problems.

But I wouldn’t equate that with a guarantee that scaling language models alone gets us to superhuman intelligence. For me, the interesting question is what happens when you combine that foundation with learning through interaction. Can the model propose solutions, test them, get feedback, and improve? In domains where you can verify an answer, there’s an opportunity to learn beyond simply imitating what humans have written down.

And human performance isn’t necessarily a ceiling for that process. A system can learn from human knowledge initially, then explore possibilities that we haven’t explored. The difficult part is making that work across open-ended tasks, where success is harder to measure and feedback is less reliable.

So I see foundation models as a plausible starting point: they give us a very broad base of capabilities. The path beyond that may depend on how we enable them to experiment, reason, and keep learning.

r001.rationale: It says human performance need not be a ceiling, but does not identify human intelligence as proof that general intelligence is possible.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning from human knowledge and written material, but not learning what humans find interesting from internet-scale data.

r003.rationale: It does not say that learned notions of human interest can prune an AI’s exploration space.

r004.rationale: It discusses proposing and testing solutions, but not combining variation generation with selection of interesting variants for open-ended self-improvement.

r005.rationale: It mentions verifiable answers and feedback, but does not establish empirical evidence as necessary to ground the proposed variation-and-selection process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that we’ve found a way to build systems that keep getting more capable as we scale them. We’re not having to hand-design a separate solution for every task. We train a model on a very broad distribution of data, and it learns representations and capabilities that transfer to problems it hasn’t explicitly been trained to solve.

That’s a powerful starting point. But I wouldn’t equate predicting the next token with having solved intelligence. There are still questions around reasoning, planning, interacting with the world, and learning from the consequences of your actions. What makes foundation models exciting is that they can provide a substrate for those things. You can put them in a loop where they act, receive feedback, and improve, rather than only learn from a fixed dataset of human-generated examples.

For me, the possibility of going beyond human performance comes from that combination: broad knowledge learned at scale, together with the ability to explore and learn from experience. It’s a plausible path, rather than a guarantee, and there’s still a lot of research needed to understand how far it can take us.
